cards.title: Floorplan before any shape
cards.text:
# Floorplan before any shape

tags: floorplan, aspect, area, signal-flow

Decide the floorplan on paper, in one pass, the way a designer does, and then generate it.
Do not discover the floorplan by placing devices and deleting them.

- Signal flow left to right. Power rails on the long edges.
- Every block, not only the top cell, aims at square (1:1). 1.5:1 is a warning. 2:1 fails
  the audit. A long row is a failed floorplan: fold it (two rows of ABBA, not one ABBAABBA).
- Write an area budget first: device area times about 1.5-2.5 for routing. Utilisation under
  ~30 % means the empty space is wire.
- Only a standard-cell-height leaf (one inverter, one flip-flop) may be a thin row, and those
  leaves are tiled into a square logic block.
- Fast blocks (comparator, sampler, clock) sit so their critical nets are short. Slow blocks
  (bias) care about matching and area, not about a femtofarad.

Source: Hastings, *The Art of Analog Layout*, 2nd ed. (2006), floorplanning and matching;
measured failure in this project: phase-1 SAR layouts that were one long row.

cards.title: Matching: centroid, interdigitation, dummies
cards.text:
# Matching: centroid, interdigitation, dummies

tags: matching, common-centroid, ABBA, dummy, interdigitate, mirror

Matched devices are identical instances of one PDK pcell: same master, W, L, fingers,
orientation. A ratio is a count of unit fingers, never a different finger width.

- A pair that must reject a gradient is common-centroid: ABBA in one row, or a 2-D
  cross-coupled ABAB / BABA. The centroids coincide. `laygrid.common_centroid` and
  `laygrid.cross_coupled` build the pattern; you choose which pattern.
- A ratioed mirror is interdigitated unit fingers (ABAB), not two transistors of different width.
- Every matched row starts and ends with a dummy, tied off (gate to source or to a rail),
  so every real unit has the same neighbours. Capacitor arrays get the same ring of dummies.
- One symmetry axis for the whole differential circuit. Both halves use the same orientation
  family (mirror, not a rotated copy that sees a different stress).

Source: Hastings, 2nd ed. (2006); Baker, *CMOS Circuit Design, Layout, and Simulation*.
Check: `scripts/layout_audit.py --pairs-from tb.scs` and `--groups`.

cards.title: Devices are PDK instances, never drawings
cards.text:
# Devices are PDK instances, never drawings

tags: pcell, instantiation, mosfet, fingers, cdf

A MOSFET, resistor, or capacitor in the layout is an instance of the PDK pcell, with CDF
parameters (finger width, length, fingers, multiplier). It is not a set of diffusion,
poly, and metal rectangles you drew.

- Look up the cell name in the PDK library. Do not hard-code a device from a different kit,
  and do not assume one kit's `w` is total width. Sizing is finger width and finger count.
- Multi-finger devices share source and drain. That sharing is the pcell's job. Do not draw
  it, and do not stretch the pcell to "make it match" — change the parameters or the count.
- `laygrid.Template(lib, cell, params={...})` then `tech.measure`. Pin names come back from
  the pcell (`G`, `S`, `D`, and the PDK's per-finger names). Read `tpl.pins`. Do not guess them.
- Hand-drawn device geometry is a failed layout even if DRC is clean.

Source: Hastings, 2nd ed., MOS transistor layout (multi-finger, unit elements); Clein,
*CMOS IC Layout* (use the device cells the kit provides).

cards.title: Capacitor arrays (the CDAC)
cards.text:
# Capacitor arrays (the CDAC)

tags: capacitor, CDAC, unit-cap, mim, common-centroid, dummy

A DAC or a matched capacitor is an array of identical unit capacitors, not one drawn plate
per code and not a single large device per bit.

- One unit pcell. Bit k is 2^k copies of that unit, in a common-centroid or interdigitated
  map, with dummies around the array. The two differential halves mirror each other.
- The top plate (the sensitive node) is shielded: grounded metal beside or over the routing
  that leaves the array, and no clock routed parallel to it. A wire on that node is budgeted
  at about 0.1-0.2 fF per micrometre of minimum-width metal; if the wire approaches the unit
  capacitance, move the array, do not add a fudge capacitor in the schematic.
- Route the bottom plates on the grid, same length per unit as far as the pattern allows.
  Series resistance of the bottom plate is part of settling. Wider metal or more vias, still
  on pitch, not a hand-drawn pour that leaves the grid.
- The array is its own cell, nearly square, instantiated in the ADC. It is not a strip down
  the side of the chip. Phase-2 runs that left the CDAC at ~2.7:1 failed this.

Source: Hastings, 2nd ed., capacitor layout and matching; LAYGO's template-and-grid arrays
(`references/laygrid.md`).

cards.title: Metal grid: one direction per layer
cards.text:
# Metal grid: one direction per layer

tags: metal, grid, pitch, preferred-direction, manhattan, routing

Interconnect is a grid. It is not a polyline you adjust until DRC passes.

- Adjacent metals run in opposite directions. If the PDK document names the directions, use
  those. If it does not, Metal1 horizontal, Metal2 vertical, and alternate. Never both
  directions on one layer "just this once."
- Pitch is whatever laygrid measured: via landing plus the minimum spacing, widened if the
  techfile's width table says so. Every wire centerline and every pin center is on that pitch.
  A via can land on every track crossing. Off-grid metal is a defect, not a shortcut.
- Manhattan only. No diagonals, no arbitrary jogs. A jog is a track change through a via,
  on grid.
- Minimum width for signals. The grid pitch already fits that width. Do not neck a wire
  below the rule to squeeze a route; move a row instead.
- Pins are rectangles on the cell's routing layer, on the grid, on the cell edge, with the
  schematic's net names. Not a text label floating in the middle.

Source: Saint & Saint, *IC Mask Design* (2002); Hastings, 2nd ed., interconnect.
Tool: `Layout.tracks` and `Layout.connect` in `lib/laygrid.py`. The pitch is measured from
the techfile. No PDK number belongs in your script.

cards.title: Vias, contacts, and current
cards.text:
# Vias, contacts, and current

tags: via, contact, electromigration, current-density, array

A contact connects metal to diffusion or poly. A via connects two metals. Neither is a pad.

- One via is enough only for a tiny signal. A supply, a tail, a sampling-switch path, and
  any net that carries more than one device's current gets an array (2x2 at minimum on
  supplies). Via resistance in series with a switch is a settling error.
- Where the PDK gives a current-density or electromigration limit, width is current divided
  by that limit, then snapped up to a whole number of tracks. Where it does not, supplies
  and tails are several tracks wide and you say so in the layout script. Do not leave a
  supply on minimum width.
- Stacked vias (M1-M2-M3) are arrays at each level, landed on the grid, not a single cut
  offset to "make it fit."
- Diffusion contacts inside a pcell are the pcell's. Do not delete them, and do not confuse
  them with bond pads.

Source: Hastings, 2nd ed., current density, contact and via resistance.

cards.title: Shielding and what may run next to what
cards.text:
# Shielding and what may run next to what

tags: shield, coupling, clock, analog, crosstalk

Coupling is planned, not discovered in a post-layout sim and patched with a random shield.

- Sensitive nets: comparator inputs, CDAC top plate, bias, sample-and-hold. Clocks and
  digital run on an upper metal, cross those nets at right angles, and do not run parallel
  to them. A long parallel run is a redraw of the floorplan.
- Shield a sensitive run with grounded metal on both sides on the same layer, or with a
  grounded plane on the layer above, tied down with a via array often enough that the shield
  is not itself a floating antenna. Ground means the analog quiet rail, not a clock buffer's
  local supply.
- Differential pairs are routed as a matched pair: same layer, same length, same via count,
  same neighbour on the outside. The match of the parasitics matters as much as their size.
- For a sampling switch, a cross-coupled dummy metal can cancel input-to-hold coupling.
  That dummy is drawn in the generator, symmetric, not added after a sim looks bad.

Source: Hastings, 2nd ed., coupling and shielding; LAYGO TI-SAR practice already noted in
`references/layout-guidelines.md`.

cards.title: Rails, taps, and guard rings
cards.text:
# Rails, taps, and guard rings

tags: power, rail, tap, substrate, well, guard-ring, latchup

- VDD and VSS are wide rails on the long edges of each row, on a thick metal, on the grid.
  Analog and digital supplies are separate nets even when they share a voltage. Do not strap
  them together inside the block to "make LVS easier."
- Every row has well taps and substrate taps along it, at the spacing the latch-up rule
  requires (the techfile; if you have not read it, the conservative practice is a tap every
  few tens of micrometres, not one tap in the corner). Taps are pcells or the kit's contact
  cells, tied to the right rail.
- A sensitive analog block (comparator, CDAC, bias) gets a guard ring: a continuous
  substrate or well contact around it, tied to a quiet rail. Digital sits outside that ring.
- The ring is part of the generator for that cell, not a rectangle added the hour before tapeout.

Source: Hastings, 2nd ed., wells, substrate contacts, guard rings; Clein, *CMOS IC Layout*.

cards.title: Differential symmetry
cards.text:
# Differential symmetry

tags: symmetry, differential, mirror, routing-match

- One axis. Every pair in the block shares it. `layout_audit` warns when the axes disagree.
- Mirror the placement. Route both halves with the same script (same tracks, mirrored), so
  the parasitics match. A via on one side only is a mismatch.
- Do not mirror by copying a finished layout and flipping it in the GUI. The generator
  places both halves. A later hand edit is applied to both halves or to neither.
- The comparator sits on the axis between the two capacitor halves. That is why the CDAC is
  two square-ish arrays, not one wide bar with the comparator at the end.

Source: Hastings, 2nd ed., matching under gradients; this project's phase-2 floorplans.

cards.title: Hierarchy: leaf, then place
cards.text:
# Hierarchy: leaf, then place

tags: hierarchy, leaf-cell, instantiate

- Lay out a leaf (a fingered transistor row, a latch, a unit capacitor, a logic gate) and
  instantiate it. The top cell is instances, rails, and routes between pins. It is not
  hundreds of raw transistors.
- The schematic's hierarchy is the layout's hierarchy. A new layout cell that has no
  schematic cell will not LVS as that cell; do not invent layout-only hierarchy that the
  netlist cannot name.
- A generator per cell, `layout_<cell>.py`, calls the leaf generators or places the leaf
  cells. One script, one cell.

Source: Clein, *CMOS IC Layout*, hierarchical mask design; BAG / LAYGO template composition
(`references/laygrid.md`).

cards.title: A block is not a chip
cards.text:
# A block is not a chip

tags: pad, bond-pad, io-ring, seal-ring, esd, adc

This ADC is a block that will sit inside a larger chip. It does not get a pad frame.

Forbidden on the block, even if a textbook chapter shows them (those chapters are about the
chip):

- bond pads, probe pads, pad openings
- an I/O ring or a seal ring
- ESD clamps on the pins
- fill or logo that exists only because a die needs it

Pins are internal metal pins on the routing grid, named as in the schematic.

Still required, and not pads: diffusion contacts, poly contacts, vias, substrate taps, well
taps, guard rings. "No contact pads" means no bond pads. It does not mean delete contacts.

Source: Hastings and Baker treat the pad frame as chip-level. A block that includes one is
the wrong component, and the pad capacitance is not in the schematic.

cards.title: When a simulation is allowed
cards.text:
# When a simulation is allowed

tags: iteration, verify, pex, testbench, generator

Simulation checks a decision you already made. It is not the search.

Allowed:

1. Operating-point check of the schematic before any layout (`scripts/opcheck.py`).
2. One DRC after the generator runs. Fix the script, run again. Do not fix by painting shapes.
3. One post-layout check of a fast leaf (comparator, sampler, clock) when that generator is
   DRC-clean and LVS-clean. Read the worst-net list (`scripts/netbrief.py pex` or verify's
   summary). Change the floorplan or the wire budget in the script and regenerate.
4. One short top-level check (<= 16 conversions, typical corner) after the blocks are in.
5. One long top-level check, both corners, at the end.

Not allowed: a simulation after each wire, a Monte-Carlo to decide a nudge, reading a
waveform into the conversation, re-running an unchanged netlist.

A layout that meets spec after dozens of hand nudges is still a failed method. Rewrite the
generator so the next person can regenerate it.

Source: this project's measured cost (top-level post-layout was 45-80 min before the short
testbench) and Hastings' practice of finishing the floorplan before drawing.

cards.title: The only layout flow: LAYGO2, implemented here by laygrid
cards.text:
# The only layout flow: LAYGO2, implemented here by laygrid

tags: laygo, laygo2, bag, generator, template, grid, route, place

Do not place shapes by hand and do not install a second layout tool. The flow is the
one in laygo2 (https://laygo2.github.io/overview.html). In this repository it is
`lib/laygrid.py`. Map their steps onto these calls:

| laygo2 | here |
|---|---|
| `load_templates()`, `load_grids()` | `Tech.load`, then `Template` of a PDK pcell, then `tech.measure` |
| `Template.generate()` | one measured template per device size |
| `Design.place()` | `Layout.row` with `common_centroid`, `interdigitate`, `cross_coupled`, `with_dummies` |
| `Design.route()`, `route_via_track()` | `Layout.tracks` then `Layout.connect` |
| `Design.pin()` | pin shapes on the routing layer, on the grid, at the cell edge, schematic names |
| `export` (SKILL / skillbridge / GDS) | `Layout.write` into the open Virtuoso, then `scripts/verify.py` |
| save as a template and reuse | the leaf cell is instantiated in the parent generator. Do not flatten it |

What the papers require, in this order:

1. **Templates on a placement grid** (Han et al., IEEE TCAS-I, March 2021, DOI
   10.1109/TCSI.2020.3046524). A template encapsulates the device and the design rules.
   You place templates by relative position on the grid, not by absolute coordinates you
   guessed. The grid is process-specific and is measured from the techfile.
2. **Wires on a routing grid.** Same paper: interconnect is on-grid so the design rules
   stay inside the grid, including multi-pattern coloring when the techfile has mask
   colors. A differential pair and its shields are generated from the same abstract
   tracks (same length, same via count, shields beside the pair). They are not drawn
   after a simulation looks bad.
3. **One Python generator per cell**, then export. laygo2's design flow is load, generate,
   place, route, pin, export, and optionally reuse the cell as a template. Final touches
   are a few shapes after that export is DRC-clean. If you are looping in the GUI, you
   have left the flow.
4. **Layout-aware, not schematic-then-hope** (Guo et al., BAG3++, IEEE OJCAS, 2025, DOI
   10.1109/OJCAS.2024.3502641). Their SAR ADC is a generator: capacitor DAC, sampler,
   logic, then extracted simulation of that layout. Digital place-and-route is the wrong
   tool for the fast analog cells (it forces standard-cell shapes and ignores the
   parasitics that dominate). Extract the fast leaf before assembling the ADC.

The TI-SAR in the LAYGO paper is a full chip with its own pads. This project's ADC is a
block. Follow their generator and grid. Do not follow their pad frame. See `11-not-a-chip.md`.
